content: The primary complication associated with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) shunt surgery is infection of the shunt. To prevent these infections, antibiotics can be administered in five distinct ways: orally, intravenously, intrathecally, topically, or through the use of antibiotic-impregnated shunt catheters. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of these different routes of antibiotic prophylaxis in reducing the incidence of CSF shunt infections in patients with internalized CSF shunts used to treat hydrocephalus. A systematic electronic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and Embase, without restrictions on language, date, or publication type. This search was performed in January 2018 with the assistance of an information specialist. The inclusion criteria were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that investigated the effects of antibiotic prophylaxis, regardless of dose or route of administration, on the prevention of CSF shunt infections in patients with internal CSF shunts. Studies involving external shunts were excluded. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers, and disagreements were resolved through discussion or consultation with an independent researcher. Analyses were conducted by at least two authors to ensure accuracy. The systematic review included 11 small randomized controlled trials with a total of 1109 participants. Three of these studies exclusively involved children, while the remaining eight included participants of all ages. Most studies focused on ventriculoperitoneal shunts, although five studies included participants with ventriculoatrial shunts, and one study involved four participants with subduroperitoneal shunts. Of the 11 trials, four (36%) were judged to have an unclear risk of bias, while seven (64%) were deemed to have a high risk of bias in one or more assessed components. The analysis of all included studies suggested that antibiotic prophylaxis might reduce the incidence of shunt infections, with a relative risk (RR) of 0.55 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.36 to 0.84). This indicates a 55% reduction in the risk of shunt infections compared to standard care or placebo. However, the quality of evidence was low. When examining specific routes of administration, only intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis showed potential evidence of reducing the risk of shunt infections, with a relative risk of 0.55 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.90) based on eight studies involving 797 participants. Evidence for intrathecal administration was uncertain, with a relative risk of 0.73 (95% CI 0.28 to 1.93) based on two studies with 797 participants and low-quality evidence. Similarly, evidence for antibiotic-impregnated catheters was also uncertain, with a relative risk of 0.36 (95% CI 0.10 to 1.24) based on one study with 110 participants and very low-quality evidence. In conclusion, antibiotic prophylaxis may reduce the incidence of shunt infections, but the quality of the included studies was low, and the effect was inconsistent across different routes of administration. It remains unclear whether the prevention of shunt infections varies based on the type of antibiotic, route of administration, timing, dosage, or patient characteristics (e.g., children versus adults). The findings of this review should be considered hypothesis-generating rather than definitive. Further research, including adequately powered trials or large multicenter studies, is needed to provide high-quality evidence in the field of ventricular shunt infection prevention.
